events.label: 13.8 billion years ago
events.title: Big Bang
events.detail: The universe begins expanding from a hot, dense state. Planck satellite data put its age at 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years; the atoms that will build Earth are mostly forged later, inside generations of stars.

sources.title: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641 A6 – Planck 2018 results VI: Cosmological parameters
NASA WMAP – How old is the universe?

events.label: 4.57 billion years ago
events.title: Sun ignites
events.line: Dust disk around a newborn star
events.detail: The oldest solids in the Solar System, calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions in meteorites, date to 4,567.3 ± 0.16 million years ago. Dust and planetesimals in the disk around the young Sun begin colliding and sticking together.

sources.title: Connelly et al. 2012, Science – The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk
NASA – Sun facts

events.label: 4.54 billion years ago
events.title: Earth forms
events.detail: Earth assembles from colliding planetesimals. Radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial and lunar samples gives an age of 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years.

sources.title: USGS – Age of the Earth

events.label: 4.51 billion years ago
events.title: Theia impact
events.detail: A Mars-sized body, often called Theia, strikes the young Earth; debris thrown into orbit gathers into the Moon. Zircons from Apollo 14 samples imply the Moon formed by about 4.51 billion years ago. The giant-impact model is the leading explanation, though its details are still debated.

sources.title: Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature – Origin of the Moon in a giant impact near the end of the Earth's formation
Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances – Early formation of the Moon 4.51 billion years ago
NASA – How the Moon formed

events.label: 4.5 billion years ago
events.title: Magma ocean
events.detail: Energy from the giant impact melts much of the planet, leaving a global ocean of magma under a thick, hot atmosphere. As it cools and crystallises, Earth's mantle and early atmosphere take shape.

sources.title: Elkins-Tanton 2012, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences – Magma oceans in the inner solar system

events.label: 4.4 billion years ago
events.title: First oceans
events.line: Water pools on a cooling crust
events.detail: A detrital zircon crystal from the Jack Hills, Western Australia, is 4.404 billion years old, and its oxygen isotopes point to liquid water at the surface. Earth may have had oceans within about 150 million years of forming.

sources.title: Wilde et al. 2001, Nature – Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago
Mojzsis et al. 2001, Nature – Oxygen-isotope evidence from ancient zircons for liquid water at the Earth's surface 4,300 Myr ago
Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience – Hadean age for a post-magma-ocean zircon confirmed by atom-probe tomography

events.label: About 3.9 billion years ago
events.title: Heavy bombardment
events.detail: Lunar impact-melt ages cluster around 4.1–3.8 billion years ago, which was read as a spike in impacts across the inner Solar System. Whether this was a true cataclysm or the tail of a slowly declining bombardment is debated.

sources.title: Bottke & Norman 2017, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences – The Late Heavy Bombardment

events.label: 3.48 billion years ago
events.title: First life
events.detail: Stromatolites and microbial textures in 3.48-billion-year-old hot-spring rocks of the Dresser Formation, Western Australia, are among the oldest widely accepted signs of life. Older claims, such as 3.7-billion-year-old structures in Greenland, are contested.

sources.title: Djokic et al. 2017, Nature Communications – Earliest signs of life on land preserved in ca. 3.5 Ga hot spring deposits
Allwood et al. 2006, Nature – Stromatolite reef from the Early Archaean era of Australia
Nutman et al. 2016, Nature – Rapid emergence of life shown by discovery of 3,700-million-year-old microbial structures
Allwood et al. 2018, Nature – Reassessing evidence of life in 3,700-million-year-old rocks of Greenland

events.label: About 2.6 billion years ago
events.title: Hazy skies
events.detail: Sulphur and carbon isotopes from South African rocks suggest that, between about 2.65 and 2.5 billion years ago, Earth's oxygen-poor, methane-rich atmosphere repeatedly flipped into a state with a hydrocarbon haze, like Saturn's moon Titan. The evidence is indirect, so the idea is debated.

sources.title: Zerkle et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience – A bistable organic-rich atmosphere on the Neoarchaean Earth

events.label: 2.5 billion years ago
events.title: Continents rise
events.detail: Oxygen isotopes in shales record a sharp shift around 2.5 billion years ago, interpreted as large continents emerging above sea level and a modern-style water cycle switching on.

sources.title: Bindeman et al. 2018, Nature – Rapid emergence of subaerial landmasses and onset of a modern hydrologic cycle 2.5 billion years ago

events.label: 2.43 billion years ago
events.title: Great Oxidation
events.detail: Oxygen made by photosynthetic microbes first accumulates in the atmosphere around 2.43 billion years ago. Oxygen levels then fluctuated and became permanently established only around 2.22 billion years ago.

sources.title: Poulton et al. 2021, Nature – A 200-million-year delay in permanent atmospheric oxygenation

events.label: 1 billion years ago
events.title: Rodinia
events.detail: Collisions between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago gather nearly all continental blocks into the supercontinent Rodinia, which rifts apart between about 825 and 740 million years ago. With no land plants yet, the land is bare rock and sediment.

sources.title: Li et al. 2008, Precambrian Research – Assembly, configuration, and break-up history of Rodinia: A synthesis

events.label: 717 million years ago
events.title: Snowball Earth
events.detail: The Sturtian glaciation lasts from about 717 to 660 million years ago. Glacial deposits formed at tropical latitudes show that ice reached the equator, as the snowball Earth hypothesis predicts.

sources.title: Rooney et al. 2015, Geology – A Cryogenian chronology: Two long-lasting synchronous Neoproterozoic glaciations
Hoffman et al. 2017, Science Advances – Snowball Earth climate dynamics and Cryogenian geology-geobiology

events.label: About 640 million years ago
events.title: Second snowball
events.detail: A second global glaciation, the Marinoan, ends 635 million years ago after lasting at least 4 million years. Its start is less certain, with estimates from about 657 to 639 million years ago. The ice-free interval between the two snowballs lasted 20 million years or less.

sources.title: Rooney et al. 2015, Geology – A Cryogenian chronology: Two long-lasting synchronous Neoproterozoic glaciations
Prave et al. 2016, Geology – Duration and nature of the end-Cryogenian (Marinoan) glaciation
Hoffman et al. 2017, Science Advances – Snowball Earth climate dynamics and Cryogenian geology-geobiology

events.label: 539 million years ago
events.title: Cambrian explosion
events.detail: The Cambrian Period begins 538.8 ± 0.2 million years ago. Over the next tens of millions of years, fossils of most major animal groups appear abruptly, although molecular clocks suggest the groups themselves diverged earlier. The land is still bare.

sources.title: International Commission on Stratigraphy – International Chronostratigraphic Chart
Erwin et al. 2011, Science – The Cambrian conundrum: early divergence and later ecological success in the early history of animals

events.label: 472 million years ago
events.title: Plants on land
events.line: The first green on the continents
events.detail: Cryptospores from Argentina, about 473–471 million years old, are the oldest direct fossil evidence of plants on land. Molecular clocks suggest land plants originated earlier, between the middle Cambrian and the Early Ordovician.

sources.title: Rubinstein et al. 2010, New Phytologist – Early Middle Ordovician evidence for land plants in Argentina (eastern Gondwana)
Morris et al. 2018, PNAS – The timescale of early land plant evolution

events.label: 386 million years ago
events.title: First forests
events.detail: Fossil root systems in a Middle Devonian soil at Cairo, New York, about 386 million years old, mark the oldest known forest. They include Archaeopteris, whose deep, extensive roots resemble those of modern seed plants.

sources.title: Stein et al. 2020, Current Biology – Mid-Devonian Archaeopteris roots signal revolutionary change in earliest fossil forests

events.label: 252 million years ago
events.title: Pangaea
events.detail: Most land is joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean. At the end of the Permian, 251.9 million years ago, the largest mass extinction in Earth's history wipes out most marine species. Pangaea starts breaking apart roughly 200 million years ago.

sources.title: Burgess et al. 2014, PNAS – High-precision timeline for Earth's most severe extinction
USGS – This Dynamic Earth: Historical perspective

events.label: 66 million years ago
events.title: Chicxulub impact
events.detail: An asteroid roughly 10 km across hits what is now the Yucatán Peninsula, leaving a crater about 180 km wide. It triggers the mass extinction that ends the non-avian dinosaurs, dated to 66.043 ± 0.011 million years ago.

sources.title: Renne et al. 2013, Science – Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Schulte et al. 2010, Science – The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary

events.label: 34 million years ago
events.title: Antarctica freezes
events.detail: At the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, about 34 million years ago, a continental ice sheet rapidly grows over Antarctica. Climate models link it to falling atmospheric CO₂.

sources.title: DeConto & Pollard 2003, Nature – Rapid Cenozoic glaciation of Antarctica induced by declining atmospheric CO2

events.label: 2.58 million years ago
events.title: Ice ages begin
events.detail: The Quaternary Period begins 2.58 million years ago, as large ice sheets start to grow and shrink repeatedly over the Northern Hemisphere. By now the continents are close to their present positions.

sources.title: Gibbard et al. 2010, Journal of Quaternary Science – Formal ratification of the Quaternary System/Period with a base at 2.58 Ma
International Commission on Stratigraphy – International Chronostratigraphic Chart

events.label: 21,000 years ago
events.title: Last Glacial Maximum
events.detail: Between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago ice sheets reach their greatest extent, covering much of North America and northern Europe. Global sea level falls roughly 125–134 m below today's, exposing land bridges such as Beringia.

sources.title: Clark et al. 2009, Science – The Last Glacial Maximum
Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS – Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene

events.label: 11,700 years ago
events.title: Holocene begins
events.line: The ice retreats; a stable climate
events.detail: The current warm interval, the Holocene, formally begins 11,700 years before 2000 CE, defined in a Greenland ice core. Ice sheets retreat toward their present size and sea level rises.

sources.title: Walker et al. 2009, Journal of Quaternary Science – Formal definition and dating of the GSSP for the base of the Holocene
International Commission on Stratigraphy – International Chronostratigraphic Chart

events.title: Industrial era
events.detail: Burning coal, and later oil and gas, begins to raise atmospheric CO₂ from its pre-industrial level of about 280 ppm. The IPCC uses 1850–1900 as its pre-industrial baseline for global warming.

sources.title: IPCC AR6 WG1 – Summary for Policymakers (2021)
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory – Trends in atmospheric CO2

events.label: 4 October 1957
events.title: Sputnik 1
events.detail: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58 cm sphere that circled Earth every 96 minutes; the space age, and Earth's population of satellites, begins here.

sources.title: NASA History – Sputnik and the origins of the Space Age

events.label: 20 November 1998
events.title: Space station begins
events.line: Zarya, the first ISS module, launches
events.detail: A Proton rocket launched Zarya; two weeks later Space Shuttle Endeavour brought Unity, and assembly of the International Space Station began.

sources.title: NASA – High-flying construction: building the ISS
NASA – STS-88

events.label: 2 November 2000
events.title: Always someone up there
events.detail: Bill Shepherd, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev docked in a Soyuz; people have lived aboard the ISS continuously ever since.

sources.title: NASA – Expedition 1 arrives at the ISS

events.label: July 2011
events.title: ISS assembly complete
events.line: The last Space Shuttle flight, STS-135
events.detail: With the final Shuttle missions the station reached its full span of 109 m, about the length of a football pitch, and some 420 tonnes.

sources.title: NASA – STS-135, the Space Shuttle's grand finale
NASA – Space station facts and figures

events.label: 24 May 2019
events.title: Starlink begins
events.detail: SpaceX launched its first 60 Starlink satellites. By 26 October 2026 it had launched 13,042, of which 11,166 are still in orbit, more than all other active satellites combined.

sources.title: Jonathan McDowell – Starlink statistics

events.label: 31 May 2020
events.title: Dragon brings astronauts
events.line: Demo-2 docks: the first crewed Dragon
events.detail: Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken docked Crew Dragon Endeavour to the forward port of Harmony, the first crew to reach orbit on a commercial spacecraft.

sources.title: NASA – Crew Dragon docks to space station

events.title: Today
events.detail: About 8.3 billion people live on Earth (UN World Population Prospects 2024 projection for 2026). Global-average CO₂ reached 425.6 ppm in 2025 (NOAA). 2024 was the warmest year on record, about 1.55 °C above pre-industrial, and 2025 was about 1.43 °C above (WMO).

sources.title: UN DESA – World Population Prospects 2024
Our World in Data – Population with UN projections
NOAA GML – Global annual mean CO2
WMO – 2024 confirmed as warmest year on record at about 1.55°C above pre-industrial level
IISD SDG Knowledge Hub – WMO State of the Global Climate 2025 report (23 March 2026)

events.title: First commercial station
events.line: Vast Haven-1, launched on a Falcon 9
events.detail: Vast's single-module Haven-1, 10.1 m long, is planned for a 425 km, 51.6° orbit, hosting four crew for two-week visits; it has not launched yet.

sources.title: Vast – Haven-1

events.title: The ISS starts down
events.line: Its orbit is allowed to sink
events.detail: From early to mid-2028 NASA expects drag and Russian-segment thruster burns to begin lowering the station, ahead of a controlled re-entry.

sources.title: GAO-26-107805 – ISS transition

events.label: Mid-2029
events.title: SpaceX's deorbit vehicle docks
events.line: A Dragon with an enlarged trunk
events.detail: NASA picked SpaceX in June 2024 (up to $843 million) to build the US Deorbit Vehicle; it is planned to launch and attach to the ISS in mid-2029, a decision NASA confirms in 2027.

sources.title: NASA – US Deorbit Vehicle selection
GAO-26-107805 – ISS transition

events.label: End of 2030 – early 2031
events.title: The ISS comes home
events.line: A final burn over the South Pacific
events.detail: With the crew gone, the deorbit vehicle fires to drive the station into the uninhabited South Pacific near Point Nemo; most of it burns up, surviving pieces fall to the ocean.

sources.title: NASA – ISS deorbit analysis summary
GAO-26-107805 – ISS transition

events.title: After the ISS
events.detail: Planned successors include Vast's Haven-2, Axiom Station and Starlab (on one Starship, 2029); China's Tiangong keeps flying and India plans BAS-1 for 2028. Dates are company and agency targets.

sources.title: Airbus – Starlab
Vast – Haven-2
SpaceNews – Tiangong completed

events.title: Warmer world
events.detail: IPCC AR6 projects that by 2081–2100 global temperature will be 1.0–1.8 °C above 1850–1900 under very low emissions (SSP1-1.9), 2.1–3.5 °C under intermediate emissions (SSP2-4.5), and 3.3–5.7 °C under very high emissions (SSP5-8.5). It projects 2100 sea level likely 0.28–1.01 m above 1995–2014, depending on the scenario.
events.projected_by: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers, August 2021

sources.title: IPCC AR6 WG1 – Summary for Policymakers (2021)

events.label: About 1 billion years from now
events.title: Oceans boil
events.line: A brighter Sun ends liquid water
events.detail: The Sun slowly brightens as it ages. A 3D climate model puts Earth's runaway-greenhouse threshold at about 375 W/m² of absorbed sunlight, up from about 341 W/m² today, which the authors estimate is reached in about a billion years. Beyond it, the oceans evaporate.
events.projected_by: Leconte, Forget, Charnay, Wordsworth & Pottier, Nature, December 2013

sources.title: Leconte et al. 2013, Nature – Increased insolation threshold for runaway greenhouse processes on Earth-like planets
Leconte et al. 2013 – arXiv preprint

events.label: About 5 billion years from now
events.title: Red giant
events.detail: NASA estimates the Sun has about 5 billion years left before it becomes a white dwarf; first it will swell into a red giant, engulfing Mercury and Venus and possibly Earth. One stellar-evolution model has the Sun reaching its largest red-giant size about 7.6 billion years from now, probably swallowing Earth.
events.projected_by: NASA Science (Sun facts page); Schröder & Smith, MNRAS, 2008

sources.title: NASA – Sun facts
Schröder & Smith 2008, MNRAS – Distant future of the Sun and Earth revisited
